title: Add the Same Each Step
idea: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount d every time, so term n is the first term plus n − 1 lots of d.
misconceptions: Using u₁ + nd, which counts one step too many
Finding d as the earlier term minus the later term, so a decreasing sequence gets a positive d
Confusing the position n with the value u_n

estimate.basis: 150 spoken words a minute, plus each pause, 0.8 s for each cue and 2 s for each tap question with its longer feedback line. The two figures are the two recall versions. Player turns are player-paced and not counted.

notes: builds_on is ex.foundations.pre-substitute, as in the explainer map (FAL-952), because the recall is substitution. This pilot teaches SL1.2.nth-term only, which is now the map's whole entry; finding u₁, d or n from given terms is ex.algebra.arithmetic-from-terms.

No second-method section. The map lists four methods for SL1.2.nth-term: the formula is the lesson, counting on is the concrete case in the big idea, the linear form uₙ = dn + (u₁ − d) appears in example 3(b), and the GDC table is a method explainer under plan decision 4.
Numbers in the examples come from the arithmetic-context stories in game/engine/situations/arithmetic_context.gd (fight pit rows, failing well, sandbag barricade), inside their ranges.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Righto. I'm Mags, and I keep the Ledger. Every debt, every deal, every seat sold at the fight pit.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: The pit boss wants to know how many seats are in row forty. He's been counting since sunrise. He's up to row nine.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: By the end of this you'll have it without counting a single seat.

watched.speaker: mags-the-ledger
watched.say: Quick one before we start. Tap the answer.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Twenty-six. Brackets, then the times, then the plus. Hang on to that shape. It's back in a minute.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Brackets first: eight minus one is seven. Seven threes are twenty-one. Add the five. Twenty-six. Hang on to that shape.

not_watched.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_watched.say: Quick one before we start. Tap the answer.

not_watched.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_watched.say: Put the number in where the letter was. Then work the brackets first, multiply next, and add last. So with n as eight: eight minus one is seven, seven threes are twenty-one, and five more makes twenty-six.

not_watched.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_watched.say: Hang on to that shape. It's back in a minute.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Here's the pit, from the side. Row one, at the front, has twenty-two seats. Then twenty-six, thirty, thirty-four.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Every row has four more than the one in front. A list that changes by the same amount every time is an arithmetic sequence.

board.write: arithmetic sequence: add the same amount every time

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Each number in it is a term. The term in row n is u n, so u one is twenty-two. The little number says which row. The u says how many seats.

board.write: term: uₙ is the term in position n

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Two columns in my book: which row, and what's in it. Don't mix them up.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: What you add each time is the common difference, d. Later term minus earlier term. Twenty-six minus twenty-two: d is four seats per row.

board.write: common difference: d = later term − earlier term

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Now the trick. From row one to row four, you add the four three times, not four times. Count the hops.

board.write: +4 three times: 3 steps from row 1 to row 4

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: My uncle Wal fenced a paddock once. Ten panels, so he bought ten posts. There's still a gap at the end you could drive a ute through.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: The rows are the posts and the steps are the gaps. Row n is n minus one steps from row one.

board.write: row n is n − 1 steps from row 1

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: So u n is the first term, plus n minus one lots of d.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: It's in the formula book, but you still need to know what every letter means. Half the folk out here sleep with that book under the pillow.

problem.setup: Row 1 of the fight pit has 22 seats, and each row has 4 more seats than the row in front of it. Find the number of seats in row 40.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Back to the pit boss. Row forty. Step one: write down what you're finding.

board.write: Find u₄₀, the number of seats in row 40.
board.label: Step 1: what are we finding?

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step two: put the givens in the book, with their units. First term, twenty-two seats. Common difference, four seats per row. And n is forty, because we want row forty.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step three: the formula, written down clean before any numbers touch it.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step four: substitute. Twenty-two, plus forty minus one lots of four.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: That's it. Thirty-nine hops from the front row to row forty.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Count the hops. Row one to row two is one hop. Row one to row forty is thirty-nine.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step five: work it out. Brackets first, thirty-nine. Thirty-nine fours are one hundred and fifty-six. Add the twenty-two: one hundred and seventy-eight.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Step six: say it in words, with the unit. Row forty has one hundred and seventy-eight seats.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Does it make sense? The back of the pit is the big end, so row forty should hold more than row one. It does.

board.write: Check: 178 > 22, and the back rows are the big ones ✓

intro.speaker: mags-the-ledger
intro.say: Your turn. Same job, different stand. Givens first.

fallback.setup: Row 1 of the east stand has 30 seats, and each row has 3 more seats than the row in front of it.

parts.text: Find the number of seats in row 25.

working: u₁ = 30 seats, d = 3 seats per row, n = 25

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Givens, formula, then the numbers. That's how I'd have done it.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Check your n minus one. Count the hops, not the rows.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Write the givens out first, each with its unit, and go again.

problem.setup: A failing well gives 480 litres on day 1, 465 litres on day 2 and 450 litres on day 3, and keeps falling by the same amount each day. Find how much water it gives on day 20.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Dry out there.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: A harder one. There's a well past the scrap heaps that's drying up. Day one it gave four hundred and eighty litres. Day two, four sixty-five. Day three, four fifty. What does it give on day twenty?

board.write: Find u₂₀, the litres on day 20.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Givens. u one is four hundred and eighty litres. n is twenty. You find d.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Minus fifteen. The well gives less each day, so d had better be negative.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Later minus earlier: four sixty-five take away four eighty. The water's going down, so d is negative. Minus fifteen.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Formula, then substitute. The minus sign travels with the fifteen.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Nineteen lots of minus fifteen is minus two hundred and eighty-five. Four eighty take away two eighty-five leaves one hundred and ninety-five.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: On day twenty the well gives a hundred and ninety-five litres. Less than day one, which is what a drying well does.

board.write: On day 20 the well gives 195 litres.
Check: 195 < 480, and the well is drying ✓

problem.setup: A barricade is built from sandbags in layers. Layer 1, at the bottom, has 96 sandbags, layer 2 has 92 and layer 3 has 88. The numbers of sandbags in the layers form an arithmetic sequence.

parts.text: Find an expression for uₙ in terms of n.
Hence find the number of sandbags in layer 18.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: This one's laid out like the old exam papers: parts a, b and c. Write each letter down before you start the part, so whoever marks it can find your working.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: A barricade of sandbags, in layers. Ninety-six in layer one at the bottom, ninety-two in layer two, eighty-eight in layer three. The numbers make an arithmetic sequence.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Part a says write down. Write down means the answer can stand on its own, no working needed. Ninety-two minus ninety-six. Minus four.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Part b says find, and find means show your working. Formula first. Then in go ninety-six and minus four.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Expand the bracket: minus four n, plus four. Then collect the numbers. Ninety-six and four make a hundred. So u n is a hundred minus four n.

ask.prompt: Check uₙ = 100 − 4n by putting n = 1. What should you get?

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Ninety-six. A hundred minus four. It gives the bottom layer back, so I trust it.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Put one in for n. A hundred minus four is ninety-six, and that's the bottom layer. So the expression checks out.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: And look at the number in front of n. Minus four. That's d, and it always will be, so there's a second check sitting right there.

board.write: Check: the number in front of n is −4 = d ✓

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Part c says hence. Hence means use what you've already found. Put eighteen into part b. Four eighteens are seventy-two, and a hundred minus seventy-two is twenty-eight.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Layer eighteen has twenty-eight sandbags. Fewer than the bottom layer and still more than none, so the barricade stands.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Somebody left this in my book. One line's off. Find it.

ask.prompt: Tap the line with the slip.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: That's the one. They added d forty times.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Look at the second line. How many lots of four are in it, and how many should there be?

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Here's the check that catches it. Put n equals one into their rule. Twenty-two plus one lot of four is twenty-six. That's row two. Their rule can't get the front row right, so every row comes out one row too far.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: I don't rub it out, mind. One line through it, and the right working beside it. A mistake you can still read is one you won't make twice.

intro.speaker: mags-the-ledger
intro.say: Your turn, and no help on the first go. Label your parts, and write the formula before the numbers.

fallback.setup: The first three terms of an arithmetic sequence are 13, 19 and 25.

parts.text: Find an expression for uₙ in terms of n.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Every part labelled and checked. I'd sign that.

right.speaker: mags-the-ledger
right.say: Clean books. That's what I like to see.

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Go back to part b and put n equals one in. Does the first term come back?

not_yet.speaker: mags-the-ledger
not_yet.say: Hence means use part b. Put the number into your expression.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: So. An arithmetic sequence adds the same d every time. To get term n, start at the first term and add d, n minus one times. You count the steps, not the terms.

board.write: 1. Write down u₁, d and n, with units
3. Answer in words, then check n = 1 gives u₁

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Next time, the pit boss wants every seat in the house added up, not one row. That's a series. Bring your book.

beats.speaker: mags-the-ledger
beats.say: Arithmetic sequences are the only honest traders in the Bazaar. Same difference, every single time.
